name: Chicago
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Chicago, IL | Genstone
metaDescription: Chicago rehab contractor for investors: bungalows, two-flats and greystones, Department of Buildings permits, draw-based billing and a free pre-offer review.
intro:
Chicago rewards investors who understand the building before they bid on it. A brick bungalow in Portage Park, a frame two-flat in Avondale and a greystone three-flat in Woodlawn can trade in the same general price band and still need completely different rehab budgets, because masonry condition, porch structure, sewer lines and electrical service change from block to block here more than almost anywhere else in the Midwest.

Genstone Construction is a renovation contractor built around investors. Our headquarters is in Romeoville, a straight run down I-55 from the city, and we coordinate vetted, licensed Chicago contractors, pull permits through the Department of Buildings, and assign one field manager who owns the job from demo to final billing. You see progress, photos and draw requests without standing in the gangway.

Start with the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review. Send the address before you commit capital and our estimators will price the scope, pressure-test the ARV and tell you plainly whether the numbers support your offer.
housingStock:
Most of the city's investor inventory falls into four building families, and each one carries its own rehab profile.

Workers' cottages went up from the 1870s through the 1890s in Pilsen, Bridgeport, Back of the Yards and parts of Logan Square. Many are frame, some were raised a half story to add a garden unit, and almost all have been altered several times. Expect balloon framing, sagging first-floor joists, old additions with shallow footings and plaster that has been patched over for a century.

Two-flats and three-flats, built roughly 1895 through the late 1920s, are the backbone of the South and West Sides and much of the Northwest Side. Brick and greystone versions share a common layout: stacked units, a rear wood porch stack, a full basement and a single sewer lateral. Their systems were rarely upgraded together, so it is normal to find one unit with modern wiring and the other still on knob-and-tube.

The bungalow belt, built mostly between the 1910s and 1930s, rings the city from Portage Park and Jefferson Park around through Chatham, Brainerd and West Lawn. These are solid face-brick houses with full basements, art glass, unfinished attics and low basement ceilings that make legal lower-level living space difficult.

After the war, builders filled the Southwest and far Northwest Sides with brick Georgians, Cape Cods and raised ranches in Garfield Ridge, Clearing, Ashburn and Norwood Park. These have better bones for mechanicals but bring 1950s and 1960s asbestos in floor tile, pipe wrap and siding.

For a rehab, the age spread matters more than the style. Nearly everything in the city predates 1978, so lead-safe practices are the default, and most buildings have cast-iron stacks, galvanized supply branches and clay sewer laterals that deserve a camera before you set a budget.

commonIssues.title: Tuckpointing, lintels and parapets
commonIssues.body: Chicago brick takes a beating from freeze-thaw cycles, and a century of it shows up as eroded mortar joints, rusted steel lintels pushing bricks out of line over windows, and parapet walls leaning on flat-roofed two-flats and three-flats. Masonry repairs are rarely the first thing a buyer notices, but an appraiser and a home inspector will. We price tuckpointing by elevation, flag lintels that need replacement rather than paint, and note parapets that should be rebuilt before a new roof goes on.

commonIssues.title: Basement water and sewer backup
commonIssues.body: The city runs on a combined sewer system, so heavy rain can push water back up through basement floor drains, especially on older blocks without overhead sewers. Add clay laterals with root intrusion and cracked cast iron under the slab, and finished basements become a liability. Before you plan a garden unit or a family room downstairs, we scope a sewer camera, a backwater valve or overhead conversion, and a sump where the site calls for it.

commonIssues.title: Electrical rules that change the budget
commonIssues.body: Chicago's electrical code has long required wiring to run in metal conduit rather than the plastic-sheathed cable used in most suburbs, and rewires must be performed by city-licensed electricians. That changes labor and material costs on every unit. Many two-flats still have knob-and-tube in the walls, undersized services and fuse panels, and rewiring an occupied flat takes careful sequencing. We separate service upgrades from branch rewiring in the estimate so you can see each cost clearly.

commonIssues.title: Rear wood porches
commonIssues.body: Stacked wood porches on two-flats and three-flats are a frequent code and safety issue. The city tightened porch construction requirements after a fatal 2003 porch collapse, and rotten ledger connections, undersized posts and missing footings are common on older stacks. A porch that looks serviceable can fail inspection during a permitted rehab. We evaluate whether repair is realistic or whether a new code-compliant porch, built to the city's porch guidelines, is the better line item.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and lead service lines
commonIssues.body: Almost the entire housing stock was built before 1978, so trim, windows and porch railings usually carry lead paint, and contractors must follow EPA lead-safe work rules on any disturbing work. Separately, a large share of Chicago homes are still served by lead water service lines running from the street. We plan lead-safe demo and window work, note whether the service line appears to be lead, and point you toward the city's replacement programs where they apply.

investorMarket:
Strategy in Chicago tends to follow the building type and the side of town.

On the Northwest Side, the bungalows and Georgians of Portage Park, Jefferson Park, Belmont Cragin and Dunning attract first-time buyers and young families, which makes them steady fix-and-flip inventory. Buyers there expect a finished basement or at least a dry, usable one, an updated kitchen and a second bathroom where the layout allows.

Logan Square, Avondale, Humboldt Park and Pilsen move faster and at higher finish levels. Here the play is often a full gut of a two-flat, sometimes a deconversion to a single-family home, and buyers compare your work against recent new construction on the same block.

The South Side holds much of the city's brick two-flat and bungalow inventory in Chatham, Auburn Gresham, South Shore and Washington Heights. Purchase prices leave room for BRRRR deals and long-term rental holds, provided the rehab focuses on durable systems instead of cosmetic upgrades.

The Southwest Side, including Garfield Ridge, West Lawn and Ashburn, offers solid postwar brick that suits both flips and single-family rentals with lower mechanical risk.

Far South neighborhoods such as Roseland and West Pullman carry a higher share of bank-owned and long-vacant property, where freeze damage and stripped systems drive scope.

Across all of these, Cook County property taxes and reassessment cycles affect rental math, so model taxes on the after-repair value rather than the current bill.
permits:
The City of Chicago Department of Buildings issues permits for work inside city limits. Minor repair and replacement work, such as some roofing, porch repair and like-for-like kitchen or bath updates, can often move through the Express Permit Program. Work that changes layout, adds a bathroom, alters structure, changes the number of units or finishes a basement as living space generally goes through Standard Plan Review with drawings from an Illinois-licensed architect.

The city requires general contractors to hold a Chicago general contractor license, and electrical and plumbing work must be done by trades licensed for that work in Chicago. Expect rough and final inspections for electrical, plumbing and ventilation, plus framing and final building inspections on larger scopes.

A few local wrinkles catch out-of-town investors. Properties in landmark districts such as parts of Pullman, Wicker Park or Logan Square's boulevard area need Commission on Chicago Landmarks review for exterior changes. Deconverting a two-flat or adding a unit triggers zoning review. And vacant buildings must be registered and maintained under the city's vacant building ordinance. Genstone tracks each of these in the scope so you know which path the job takes before work starts.
climate:
Chicago winters are long, and the lake adds wind and moisture near the shore. Freeze-thaw cycles drive the masonry, concrete and porch problems you see across the city, and they also limit when that work can happen. Tuckpointing, concrete flatwork and exterior painting are best scheduled between spring and fall, because mortar and concrete need warmer temperatures to cure properly.

Spring brings heavy rain and the highest risk of basement flooding, so sump, backwater valve and grading work belongs early in a rehab rather than at the end. Summers are humid, which matters for drywall finishing and for central air, now an expected feature in most flip neighborhoods.

For vacant property, winter is the danger season. A missed winterization or a furnace failure in January can split supply lines on every floor of a two-flat. We plan interior work for winter months and save exterior scope for warm weather wherever the schedule allows.

faqs.q: Do you work on two-flats and three-flats in Chicago?
faqs.a: Yes. Stacked two-flats and three-flats are a large part of what investors buy in the city, and we scope them as buildings rather than as separate units. That means looking at the shared sewer lateral, the rear porch stack, the roof and parapets, and whether each unit has its own heat and electrical service. We can phase work around an occupied unit or gut the building at once, depending on your plan and the condition we find.

faqs.q: Can you handle Chicago permits and inspections?
faqs.a: We manage permits through the City of Chicago Department of Buildings, using the Express Permit Program where the scope qualifies and coordinating architect drawings for Standard Plan Review when layout, structure or unit count changes. Our field manager schedules the inspections, keeps the permit card posted and tracks sign-offs. You receive the inspection results in your project documentation, along with lien waivers from the contractors who did the work.

faqs.q: How far does Genstone travel within the city?
faqs.a: We cover all of Chicago, from Rogers Park and Edison Park down through Beverly, Mount Greenwood and the Far South Side, along with inner-ring suburbs such as Oak Park, Cicero and Berwyn. Our headquarters is in Romeoville, and work is carried out by vetted, licensed contractors who already work in the city. Each project still has one designated field manager responsible for the schedule and quality.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay anything before work begins?
faqs.a: No. Genstone does not take upfront payment. Construction draws are tied to completed work that you can see documented, and final payment comes after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris removal, which can be a real cost on a tight city lot with alley access only, is already included in our estimates rather than added later. That matters in neighborhoods where a dumpster permit on the public way is needed.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Chicago, IL | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Chicago fix and flip rehabs for bungalows, Georgians and two-flat deconversions, priced to local comps with draw-based billing and a free pre-offer review.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Chicago
fix-flip.intro:
Flipping in Chicago is a comps game played house by house. The buyer touring a Jefferson Park bungalow has also walked through three others that week, and the buyer in Logan Square has seen the new construction going up two doors down. Your rehab has to beat the competition on the details those buyers notice, without sinking money into upgrades the neighborhood will not pay for.

Genstone prices Chicago flips against what is selling on your block, not a generic finish package. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at the masonry, sewer, electrical and porch exposure that sink margins in this city, then lays out one or more finish levels tied to an ARV. Once you close, a single field manager runs the job and you track every milestone online.

sections.h2: Matching finish level to the Chicago neighborhood
sections.body:
Finish decisions in Chicago are local to a degree that surprises newer investors. In Portage Park, Belmont Cragin and Garfield Ridge, buyers want a clean modern kitchen with quartz or a good solid-surface top, refinished original oak floors in the bungalow rooms, a full second bath where the attic or basement allows, and a dry basement with a laundry area. Spending on designer lighting or custom millwork there rarely comes back at sale.

In Logan Square, Avondale and parts of Pilsen, the bar moves up. Buyers compare your gut rehab against new construction, so they expect open layouts, a primary suite, a finished lower level with real ceiling height and modern mechanicals including central air.

We write scope with two or three finish levels when the comps support it, and we tie each level to the ARV range it targets. That way you can choose the version that fits your capital and your timeline instead of guessing at what a buyer will reward.

sections.h2: The hidden costs on a Chicago flip
sections.body:
The things that ruin Chicago flips are almost never the kitchen. They are the items a buyer's inspector finds after you list.

A clay sewer lateral full of roots, a cracked cast-iron stack under the basement slab, rusted lintels over the front windows, a rear porch with no footings, or knob-and-tube still live in one bedroom can each trigger a renegotiation or a cancelled contract. Chicago's conduit requirement for electrical work also means a rewire costs more here than in the suburbs, so it has to be in the budget from day one.

Our estimators look for these items during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and price them as line items, not contingencies. We also flag work that needs a full permit through Standard Plan Review, since that path takes longer than an Express Permit and affects your carrying costs. Knowing it upfront lets you adjust your offer instead of absorbing the surprise later.

Two Chicago-specific value plays show up again and again in our flip work.

The first is the bungalow basement. Finishing it can add real living space, but low ceilings, floor drains tied into a combined sewer and seepage through old foundation walls all have to be addressed first. A backwater valve or overhead sewer, waterproofing on the problem walls and egress planning come before drywall. Done right, a dry lower-level family room and full bath are among the most visible upgrades in a bungalow belt listing.

The second is the two-flat deconversion in neighborhoods where single-family buyers pay more for space than investors pay for rent. Converting a two-flat to one home involves zoning review, removing a kitchen, opening a stair and rerouting mechanicals. We scope these with drawings, sequence the permit, and compare the deconversion ARV against a straightforward two-unit renovation so you can pick the stronger exit. On blocks where both paths pencil out, the decision usually comes down to your timeline and appetite for a longer permit.

faqs.q: What kind of Chicago houses do you flip most often?
faqs.a: Brick bungalows and postwar Georgians on the Northwest and Southwest Sides make up a large share, because they have solid structure and a deep buyer pool. We also take on frame cottages, greystones and two-flats that are being renovated as two units or converted to a single home. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review tells you which version of the house the local comps support before you buy it.

faqs.q: Can you help me decide between a light and a full rehab?
faqs.a: Yes. When the comps justify it, we write the scope at more than one finish level and tie each one to an ARV. A light refresh in Belmont Cragin and a full gut in Avondale are very different plans, and seeing them side by side, with labor, materials and draw schedule for each, makes the decision a business call rather than a guess.

faqs.q: How do draws work on a Chicago flip?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Draws are tied to completed milestones such as demo, rough mechanicals passing city inspection, drywall and finishes. Each draw is documented with photos and progress notes so you or your lender can release funds without visiting the site. Lien waivers come with payment, and final billing waits until the work is complete and approved. Hard money lenders active in Chicago generally find this format easy to work with.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Chicago, IL | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Chicago built to appraise and to last: two-flats, bungalows and greystones scoped for refinance value, rental durability and city inspection.
brrrr.intro:
Chicago is one of the few big Midwestern cities where a single purchase can give you two or three rentable units, a long-term tenant pool and an appraisal based on solid brick. That is why so many BRRRR investors focus on South Side and Northwest Side two-flats and bungalows. The catch is that the refinance only works if the rehab pushes value without burning cash on finishes that a renter will wear out.

Genstone builds Chicago BRRRR scopes around two targets at once: the appraisal you need at refinance and the durability you need for years of tenancy. Through Genstone Financial, the same family of companies can also discuss fix-and-flip financing for the purchase and a DSCR rental loan for the refi, which keeps the plan coordinated from acquisition to hold.

sections.h2: Renovating a Chicago building to the refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in Chicago lean heavily on recent sales of similar buildings nearby, and for two-flats that often means comparing your property against renovated two-flats on surrounding blocks of Chatham, Auburn Gresham or Brighton Park. The upgrades that move those comparisons are the visible, permanent ones: updated kitchens and baths in each unit, refinished hardwood, new windows, a sound roof, separate modern electrical services and separate heat.

What appraisers rarely pay for is boutique finish work, so we steer budget away from it. Instead we document the system upgrades that support value, including the new service, the replaced sewer lateral, the porch rebuilt under permit and the new boilers or furnaces. A clean package of permits, inspection sign-offs and before and after photos makes the appraiser's job easier and gives you something concrete to hand the lender.

Timing matters too. If the refinance appraisal happens in winter, an unfinished exterior, a missing porch rail or a basement still drying out from tuckpointing work will all show in the photos. We sequence the visible items so the building presents as finished on the day the appraiser arrives, even if minor punch work remains inside.

The material choices that hold up in Chicago rentals are not the same as those that sell a flip. Long hallways in two-flats and greystone flats see heavy traffic, radiators and baseboard heat sit right against walls, and winter salt and slush get tracked straight through the back porch door into the kitchen.

For that reason we typically recommend luxury vinyl plank in kitchens and back entries, refinished original hardwood in living rooms where it survives, semi-gloss paint on trim, solid-surface or quartz counters that resist chipping, and simple fixtures with parts available at any Chicago supply house. In basements, we avoid carpet entirely. We also make sure each unit's water heater, panel and shutoffs are accessible, which keeps future service calls short and tenant disruptions small.

Windows deserve special attention. Original wood double-hungs in a Chicago greystone are drafty, often painted shut and usually coated in lead paint. Replacing them with vinyl or clad units cuts heating complaints, removes a lead hazard at friction surfaces and gives the appraiser one more permanent upgrade to note.

sections.h2: Separating utilities and meeting city requirements
sections.body:
Many older Chicago two-flats and three-flats share a boiler or a single water heater, and some still have a common electrical meter for both units. That arrangement makes tenant-paid utilities impossible and depresses net income, which in turn shows up in a DSCR loan calculation.

Splitting heat into individual systems, adding separate electrical services and meters, and giving each unit its own water heater is often the most valuable work in a Chicago BRRRR project, even though tenants will never notice it. These upgrades require permits through the Department of Buildings and licensed Chicago electrical and plumbing trades, and they must be coordinated with ComEd and Peoples Gas for new meters. We schedule utility work early so it does not hold up inspections at the end of the job.

Where splitting a boiler system is not practical, for example in a greystone three-flat with original cast-iron radiators throughout, we look at alternatives such as a new high-efficiency shared boiler with the heating cost built into rent. We lay out both routes in the estimate so you can weigh the cost against the income effect before committing.

faqs.q: Which Chicago neighborhoods work for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Investors commonly run BRRRR deals on brick two-flats and bungalows in South Side areas such as Chatham, Auburn Gresham and South Shore, Southwest Side areas such as Brighton Park and Gage Park, and parts of the Northwest Side. The right block depends on recent renovated sales and rents. We are not appraisers, but our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares your scope against local comps so you can judge whether the refinance math holds.

faqs.q: Will separating utilities really matter for my refinance?
faqs.a: It often does. When tenants pay their own heat and electric, your net operating income rises, and a DSCR loan is underwritten on the property's income rather than your personal earnings. Separate meters and heating systems also make the building more marketable later. The work is permitted and requires utility coordination, so we include it in the scope and draw schedule from the beginning.

faqs.q: Can Genstone help with BRRRR financing?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers fix-and-flip loans for acquisition and rehab, DSCR rental loans for long-term holds, lines of credit and new construction loans. Using it is optional. If you work with another lender, we provide the scope, estimate, draw schedule and progress documentation their inspectors need to release funds. Either way, the scope is written with the refinance appraisal on a Chicago brick building in mind.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Chicago, IL | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Chicago rental property renovation for single-family and small portfolio owners: tenant-ready turns, durable finishes and city-compliant work on older brick.
rental-renovation.intro:
A Chicago rental has to survive more than tenants. It has to survive January, a combined sewer during a summer downpour, and a city inspector if a complaint is ever filed. Owners who hold single-family bungalows, Georgians and cottages across the city learn quickly that the cheapest turn is rarely the cheapest year.

Genstone renovates rental homes in Chicago for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners with a standard approach: fix the systems that generate emergency calls, use materials that can be cleaned and repaired fast, and document everything so the next turn starts from a known baseline. Our field managers coordinate licensed Chicago trades, and Genstone Field Services can handle turns, inspections and occupied maintenance once the rehab is done.

sections.h2: A portfolio standard built for Chicago houses
sections.body:
Owners with several Chicago rentals benefit from a written standard, so every bungalow or Georgian in the portfolio ends up with the same paint colors, flooring, fixtures, appliance packages and hardware. That makes future repairs faster because parts are on hand and contractors know what to expect.

For Chicago houses, a good standard also covers items specific to the building type. It sets how basements are finished, often as dry, painted and sealed utility spaces rather than carpeted rooms. It describes how radiators are treated in houses still on hot water heat, what window type replaces failing wood sashes, and how back stairs and porches are maintained. We help write or refine that standard and then apply it consistently across your properties in the city and the suburbs.

A standard also speeds up approvals. When an asset manager already knows the approved flooring, the paint schedule and the appliance package, a new acquisition in Ashburn or Gage Park can move from inspection to an approved scope with fewer rounds of questions, and every house in the portfolio ends up looking and performing the same way.

sections.h2: Cutting service calls in older Chicago homes
sections.body:
Most rental emergencies in Chicago trace back to a short list of causes: sewer backups through basement floor drains, frozen pipes on exterior walls, failing boilers or furnaces, tripped breakers on overloaded circuits, and water heaters near the end of life.

A rental renovation is the right time to deal with them. We camera the sewer lateral and recommend rodding, lining or replacement as needed, add a backwater valve where basements flood, move or insulate supply lines in cold exterior walls, replace aging heating equipment and add circuits in kitchens where tenants run modern appliances. Each of those items costs less as part of a planned rehab than as a midnight call in February, and together they make a rental easier to keep occupied.

We also look at the garage and the alley side of the lot, since detached garages on Chicago lots often have failing roofs, rotted overhead doors or cracked slabs. Tenants use them daily, and a garage roof leak becomes a storage damage complaint quickly, so it belongs in the same planning conversation as the house.

Chicago enforces its building code through complaint-driven and periodic inspections, and violations on a rental can lead to fines and administrative hearings. A property that is tenant-ready should also be ready for an inspector to walk through.

We check smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, guards and handrails on stairs and porches, window operation and egress from sleeping rooms, hot water temperature, heating capacity and visible lead paint hazards on painted surfaces. Where the scope includes painting or window work on a pre-1978 house, we use lead-safe practices. When the rehab is finished, you get photos, permit sign-offs and lien waivers in one place, which helps if a tenant dispute or code issue ever comes up later.

Chicago landlords also operate under the city's Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance, which shapes how repairs and access are handled during a tenancy. That is one more reason to fix the big items while a unit is empty. Work that requires entry, noise and shutoffs is far simpler before a lease starts than after.

faqs.q: Do you renovate single-family rentals and small portfolios in Chicago?
faqs.a: Yes. We work with landlords who own a single bungalow and with funds and institutional owners managing many homes across the city and suburbs. Larger owners often benefit from a written renovation standard so finishes, fixtures and appliances match across the portfolio, which simplifies future maintenance and keeps costs predictable. We apply the same standard whether the house sits in Ashburn, Norwood Park or across the city line in Berwyn.

faqs.q: Can you renovate between tenants on a tight turnaround?
faqs.a: We schedule turns around your lease dates, sequencing trades so painting, flooring and repairs overlap where they safely can. Larger items such as heating replacement or sewer work are planned early so they do not hold up move-in. Genstone Field Services can also handle routine turns and make-ready work after the initial renovation is complete. In Chicago, we also confirm permit sign-offs are in hand before the new tenant receives keys.

faqs.q: What warranty comes with a Chicago rental renovation?
faqs.a: Genstone provides a one-year workmanship warranty on the work we perform. It covers defects in workmanship but does not cover tenant damage or normal wear and tear, which is why we recommend durable materials and clear move-in documentation for every unit we renovate. Photos taken at completion give you a baseline to compare against when the tenant moves out and the security deposit is reviewed.

multifamily-renovation.title: Two-Flat & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Chicago | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Chicago two-flat, three-flat and greystone renovations: shared systems, porch stacks, occupied-unit phasing and Department of Buildings permits for 2–4 units.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Two-Flat and Small Multifamily Renovation in Chicago
multifamily-renovation.intro:
No city in the country is more closely tied to the two-flat than Chicago. Brick and greystone two-flats and three-flats line block after block of Logan Square, Pilsen, Chatham, Little Village and Albany Park, along with the four-unit and courtyard buildings tucked in between. They are some of the most practical investments in the city and some of the most demanding to renovate, because every system is shared until someone separates it.

Genstone renovates Chicago buildings of two to four units as whole structures. Our scopes cover the roof, masonry, porch stack, sewer lateral and mechanicals that serve every unit, then the individual kitchens, baths and finishes. When a unit stays occupied, we phase the work so tenants keep heat, water and safe access throughout.

sections.h2: Shared systems in Chicago two-flats and three-flats
sections.body:
The shared elements of a Chicago two-flat or three-flat are where the real budget sits. One clay sewer lateral serves every unit. One roof, often flat with parapets, keeps them all dry. One rear porch stack provides the second exit required for each upper unit. Older buildings frequently have a single boiler and one water heater feeding everyone.

We evaluate each of these as building-level items. The lateral gets a camera, the roof and parapets get inspected for ponding and failed flashing, and the porch stack gets checked for ledger attachment, post size and footings against city porch requirements. Then we decide with you whether to keep heat shared or split it into individual systems, which affects both the rehab cost and how utilities are billed. Getting those choices right first makes the unit-level work straightforward.

Greystones add one more item: the limestone front. Spalled stone, failed joints and old patching in mismatched mortar are common, and they are the first thing a buyer or appraiser sees. Stone repair is specialized masonry work, so we price it separately from brick tuckpointing on the side and rear walls.

Many investors buy a two-flat with one unit occupied and plan to renovate the vacant one first. That is workable in Chicago, but it takes planning that a single-family rehab does not.

Water and gas shutoffs need to be scheduled and announced, especially when a shared riser or boiler is involved. Demo dust and lead-safe work in the vacant unit must be contained so it does not migrate up a shared stair or through the back porch. Electrical service upgrades may require a brief outage for the whole building. Our field manager sets these windows with you and the tenant ahead of time and keeps the common exit paths clear. In winter, we avoid any extended shutdown of a shared heating system, which can cause frozen pipes in the occupied unit within hours.

When the plan is to renovate the occupied unit later, we design the first phase with that in mind. Running new electrical feeders, plumbing risers and heating lines for the second unit during the first phase avoids opening finished walls twice and keeps the second renovation shorter for the incoming tenant.

sections.h2: Garden units, courtyards and unit count
sections.body:
Investors often ask whether they can add a garden unit in the basement of a Chicago two-flat or legalize one that already exists. The answer depends on zoning for the lot, ceiling height, egress, light and ventilation, and the city's current rules on adding dwelling units. Some neighborhoods allow conversions that were previously prohibited, while others do not, and the requirements can change.

We review the building and the zoning before you plan around an extra rent. Where an added or legalized unit is possible, we coordinate an architect, Standard Plan Review and the needed fire separation, egress windows and mechanicals. For courtyard and four-unit buildings, we also look at common hallway lighting, entry doors and intercoms, which affect both tenant safety and how the building shows to a future buyer or appraiser.

For larger courtyard properties, roof drainage and masonry along the interior courtyard walls are frequent problem spots. Water that runs off the roof and down those walls saturates brick and finds its way into the units below. We inspect gutters, downspouts and scuppers alongside the masonry so the repair addresses the source rather than the stain.

faqs.q: Can you renovate one unit while the other stays rented?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is common in Chicago. We contain dust and lead hazards in the vacant unit, schedule any water, gas or power interruptions in advance, keep common exits clear, and avoid long heating outages in cold weather. Your field manager coordinates with you on tenant notices so the occupied unit is disturbed as little as possible. Shared basements and laundry areas stay accessible wherever the work allows.

faqs.q: Should I split the heat in my Chicago two-flat?
faqs.a: Often it makes sense. Separate heating systems let tenants pay their own gas, which improves net income and DSCR loan math, and they remove a single point of failure for the building. The work involves permits, licensed trades and utility coordination for new meters. We price both options so you can compare the cost against the long-term operating benefit. Radiator buildings sometimes favor a shared boiler instead.

faqs.q: Can I add a garden unit to my building?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It depends on the zoning of the lot, the basement height, egress and the city's current rules on adding units. We review those conditions before you count on the extra rent, and if it is feasible we coordinate architect drawings and permits through the Department of Buildings. Basements that already flood need waterproofing and sewer protection before a unit makes sense, and we price that work alongside the conversion.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Chicago, IL | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Chicago for buyers, agents and lenders: bungalows and two-flats, Standard and Limited 203(k) bids, draws and city permits.
fha-203k.intro:
The FHA 203(k) loan fits Chicago unusually well. It lets an owner-occupant buy and renovate with one mortgage, and it applies to one-to-four unit properties, which means a buyer can purchase a two-flat or three-flat, live in one unit and fix up the whole building. In a city full of solid but dated bungalows and flats, that opens doors for buyers who could never qualify for both a purchase and a separate renovation loan.

Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We work with Chicago buyers, their agents and their lenders to produce bids that meet program requirements, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans, and run the work through draws tied to inspected progress.

sections.h2: Standard or Limited 203(k) for a Chicago house
sections.body:
The two versions of the loan suit different Chicago houses.

The Limited 203(k) is meant for non-structural work, capped at $75,000 in repairs. It fits a structurally sound bungalow or Georgian that needs a new kitchen and bath, refinished floors, a furnace, a roof, new windows and paint. Many houses on the Northwest and Southwest Sides land here.

The Standard 203(k) is required when the work involves structural changes, major additions, or repairs above the Limited cap, and it carries a $5,000 minimum repair amount. A two-flat with a failing porch stack, a cottage with a sagging floor system, or a building that needs a full gut and new mechanicals usually belongs in the Standard program. It requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant who writes the work write-up and inspects draws. We help buyers and agents identify which path the house needs early, before the offer deadline puts everyone under pressure.

sections.h2: Writing a bid that lenders and the consultant accept
sections.body:
A 203(k) bid has to be specific enough for a lender to underwrite and for a consultant to inspect against. Vague line items or lump sums cause delays at closing.

Genstone's estimators write itemized Chicago bids that break out each trade, specify materials, and reflect city realities such as conduit wiring, Department of Buildings permit fees and lead-safe work on pre-1978 trim. Where the HUD consultant's write-up identifies required repairs, our bid follows its structure so the documents line up. We also respond quickly to lender questions and revisions, because 203(k) closings in Chicago often run on contract deadlines that leave little slack. Contractor compliance paperwork, insurance and licensing are provided as part of the package.

Agents appreciate one more step. Before the bid is finalized, we walk through any items that the buyer wants but the program will not fund, such as luxury upgrades, so expectations are set clearly. In a Chicago bungalow, that conversation often centers on the basement: what can be finished within the loan and what has to wait.

sections.h2: After closing: permits, draws and living in the home
sections.body:
Once the loan closes, renovation funds sit in an escrow account and are released in draws as work is completed and inspected. Genstone does not ask the borrower for upfront payment; our draw schedule matches the program's release process.

We pull permits through the Department of Buildings, schedule the city's inspections and coordinate with the consultant for draw inspections on Standard loans. For buyers of two-flats who plan to live in one unit, we often sequence the owner's unit first so they can move in while the second unit is finished, provided the scope and loan terms allow it. Throughout, the buyer, agent and lender can see progress and documentation without making trips to the site, and lien waivers accompany each draw.

The program includes a contingency reserve for unforeseen conditions, and older Chicago buildings use it more often than newer suburban homes. Opening a plaster wall can reveal knob-and-tube still in service or a cracked stack. When that happens, we document the condition and price the change so the consultant and lender can approve the use of reserve funds.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan to buy a Chicago two-flat?
faqs.a: Yes. The FHA 203(k) program covers properties with one to four units, provided you live in one of them as your primary residence. That makes it a practical route for Chicago buyers who want rental income from the other unit while financing the renovation of the whole building in a single mortgage. The rent from the second unit can also help with qualifying, depending on the lender's guidelines.

faqs.q: Is Genstone an approved 203(k) contractor?
faqs.a: Yes, Genstone holds FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status. We prepare detailed, itemized bids that lenders and HUD consultants can work from, supply our licensing and insurance documentation, and run the renovation through the draw process with inspections tied to completed work. In Chicago, we also pull the required city permits and coordinate trade licensing, which lenders often ask to see before closing.

faqs.q: How do I know whether I need a Standard or Limited 203(k)?
faqs.a: If the house needs structural work, such as a porch stack rebuild, foundation repair or reframed floors, or if repairs exceed the $75,000 Limited cap, you will need the Standard program. Cosmetic and system updates on a sound house usually fit the Limited version. We can review the property with your agent early so the right loan is chosen before the offer.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Chicago | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned property renovation in Chicago for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze damage, vacant building rules, code violations and documented scopes.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Chicago
reo-renovation.intro:
Bank-owned property in Chicago comes with conditions that are rare in newer markets. A two-flat left vacant through a winter can have split pipes on both floors, a flooded basement from a sewer backup nobody was there to see, stripped copper and open code violations attached to the address. Servicers and asset managers need a contractor who can scope that reality quickly and document it thoroughly.

Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, and we are a preferred contractor for GSEs. In Chicago we coordinate licensed local trades, handle Department of Buildings permits and keep reporting consistent with what asset managers expect, from first inspection through final billing and lien waivers.

sections.h2: Vacant building conditions specific to Chicago
sections.body:
Vacant Chicago properties deteriorate in predictable ways. Winter is the main threat. If a building was not winterized, or if the heat failed after winterization was skipped, supply lines and radiators burst, ceilings come down and hardwood cups. Basements in combined-sewer neighborhoods may have taken on water repeatedly, leaving mold on framing and drywall.

Vandalism and theft are common on longer-vacant properties on the South and West Sides, with copper piping, radiators, water heaters and electrical wire removed. Rear porches decay without maintenance and may become unsafe to walk on. We document each of these conditions with photos during the initial inspection and separate emergency stabilization, such as securing openings or removing standing water, from the full renovation scope so asset managers can approve them on different timelines.

Utilities are another early hurdle. Gas and electric service may have been shut off at the meter, and restoring them often requires a pressure test, repairs to stripped piping and an inspection before ComEd or Peoples Gas will reconnect. We include those steps in the initial scope so the property can be heated and lit for trades as soon as approval comes through.

sections.h2: Vacant building registration and code compliance
sections.body:
Chicago requires owners of vacant buildings, including lenders and servicers holding foreclosed property, to register them with the city and keep them secured, insured and maintained to specific standards. Properties that slip out of compliance can draw citations and administrative hearings, and fines can accumulate against the owner of record.

Genstone's scopes take these obligations into account. We note open permits and visible violations, secure the building to the standards the city expects, address hazardous conditions such as damaged porches and exposed wiring, and keep records showing when each item was handled. Genstone Field Services can provide ongoing property preservation, inspections and code compliance work between acquisition and resale, so the property does not fall back out of compliance while the renovation is being approved.

Where the city has already issued violations on the address, we review them against the scope so the renovation clears them rather than leaving loose ends that surface at resale. Buyers' attorneys in Chicago routinely look for open violations and permits, and resolving them in advance keeps closings on track.

sections.h2: Renovating REO for resale or rental
sections.body:
The renovation strategy for a Chicago REO depends on the disposition plan. Some assets are repaired to make them financeable for owner-occupant buyers, which typically means working mechanicals, a sound roof, safe porches, functioning kitchens and baths and no peeling lead paint. Others are renovated to a rental standard for a fund or REIT, emphasizing durable finishes and separate utilities.

We write the scope to match the goal and provide clear estimates with labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one option when the disposition is still being decided. As an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, we can also help where a property will be sold to a buyer using renovation financing. Each job closes out with documentation, inspection sign-offs and lien waivers from every contractor.

Because Chicago REO inventory spans everything from a vacant cottage in West Pullman to a foreclosed three-flat in Humboldt Park, our estimators adjust the scope to the building type rather than applying a fixed checklist. That keeps repair dollars pointed at what will actually move the asset.

faqs.q: Do you work directly with servicers and asset managers in Chicago?
faqs.a: Yes. Our clients include mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, and Genstone is a preferred contractor for GSEs. We provide scopes, estimates, photo documentation and lien waivers in a format that fits asset management reporting, with a designated manager as your point of contact for each property. Bid turnaround and reporting cadence can be set to match your internal approval process.

faqs.q: Can you handle vacant building compliance in Chicago?
faqs.a: We address the physical requirements, including securing the building, correcting hazardous conditions and maintaining the property, and we document the work. Through Genstone Field Services we can also provide ongoing preservation, inspections and code compliance between acquisition and resale so the property stays in order while decisions are made. Registration filings themselves remain the owner's responsibility, and we supply the records that support them.

faqs.q: What happens when a Chicago REO has freeze damage?
faqs.a: We first stabilize it by shutting off water, removing standing water and wet materials, and drying the structure to limit mold. Then we document the damage and scope repairs, which commonly include new supply lines, drywall and ceilings, flooring and heating components. The scope separates emergency items from the full renovation so they can be approved separately. Radiator systems are pressure tested before any boiler is restarted.
